activities.title: An enforcing conditional access policy requires MFA for all users and resources
activities.description: Observes that the tenant REQUIRES a second factor, from an enforcing conditional access policy covering all users and all resources. Three residual gaps are stated rather than papered over. A policy is configuration, not evidence that any sign-in actually presented a second factor. The control scopes to services that process, store or communicate sensitive data, and the tenant does not record which of its services those are -- so "all resources" is used as the conservative proxy and a narrower, correctly-scoped policy would read here as a near miss. And every real tenant excludes break-glass accounts, so exclusions are counted against a threshold rather than forbidden; the threshold is a judgement, not an observation.

activities.title: Enabled authentication methods can form an acceptable multi-factor pair
activities.description: Observes which authentication methods the TENANT POLICY enables, which is a statement about what users may register -- not about what any user actually registered or presented at a sign-in. The control speaks to what multi-factor authentication "uses", and the gap between enabled and used is real: a tenant may permit only acceptable methods while a given account holds none of them. Closing it needs sign-in logs, which is PR 10's evidence-provider work. Factor STRENGTH is deliberately out of scope here; phishing resistance is an ML2/ML3 bar under a different control.

activities.title: Multi-factor authentication offered to customers of online customer services
activities.description: Customers are not authenticated by the corporate directory. Customer identity almost always lives in a separate estate -- a B2C tenant, a bespoke portal, or a provider's platform -- which is outside the inventory this project assesses. Answering it from the corporate tenant would describe staff, not customers, and would be wrong in the direction that matters: it would report a pass.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: The service catalogue entry for each online customer service handling sensitive customer data, recording the customer authentication design and the date it was last reviewed.

props.name: attestation-owner
props.value: Product owner for each customer-facing service

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: Customer identity is a separate estate from the corporate directory this project inventories, and is frequently operated by a provider. Deriving a verdict from corporate identity data would answer a different question about a different population of people.

activities.title: Requests for privileged access are validated when first requested
activities.description: The control is about an act of validation at a moment in the past, not about a system's current state. A directory can show that an account holds privilege; it cannot show that the request for it was validated, by whom, or against what criteria. Group membership is not evidence of approval -- treating it as such is precisely how an unapproved administrator comes to be reported as compliant.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: Privileged access request records in the service management system, showing for each grant the requester, the validating authority and the date, held for the retention period required by the agency's record-keeping policy.

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: The evidence is an approval record, not a system state. Even a perfectly instrumented directory records only the resulting membership, and a membership that exists today says nothing about whether its request was validated when it was first made.

activities.title: Privileged online-service access is limited to what duties require
activities.description:
The control compares two quantities and neither is a system state, which is what separates it from the four other privileged-access controls examined alongside it and deferred rather than attested.
"Explicitly authorised to access online services" is an approval. A security group, a proxy rule or an Entra group is the *implementation* of an authorisation decision, never the decision -- the same substitution this project already refused for ism-1507. Here it cuts deeper: for ism-1507 the approval merely produces a membership the control is about, while here the approval *defines the population the control is a statement about*, so a directory read cannot even compute the denominator.
"Only what is required for users to undertake their duties or functions" is a proportionality judgement about a person's job. No directory, PAM vault, identity governance platform, proxy or CASB holds an attribute meaning "what this person's duties require". An access review records that an approver clicked approve, which returns you to the first term. A job title is a string, not a set of required services.
What settles it is that no product implements "strictly limited to what is required" the way a conditional access policy implements "MFA is required". Where such a mechanism exists this project automates at proxy or partial confidence and accepts the ceiling; here there is no mechanism to read, which makes this structure rather than effort.
Three observables were considered and rejected on principle, not cost. Counting the authorised set against a threshold would publish a number this project invented inside an OSCAL document citing an ASD control id. Observing egress from a proxy or CASB measures what access exists, not what is authorised, and its only detectable failure belongs to ism-1175. Reading an identity-governance campaign's completion records that a review happened, not that its outcome was proportionate.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: The register of privileged user accounts explicitly authorised to access online services, recording for each account the services authorised, the business function requiring them, the approving authority and the date of the most recent proportionality review.

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: Both sides of the control's comparison are approval and judgement artefacts. The authorised population is defined by an approval decision rather than by any group membership that implements it, and "what a user's duties require" exists in no system as an attribute. No product implements the limitation the way a policy engine implements an authentication requirement, so there is no configuration state to read -- this is a gap no amount of engineering closes, not a collector nobody has written yet.

activities.title: Multi-factor authentication on third-party online customer services
activities.description: Combines both barriers at once: the service belongs to a third party, and the people being authenticated are customers rather than staff. Neither the configuration nor the population appears anywhere in the estate this project can reach.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: The third-party service register, for entries that handle sensitive customer data, recording the customer authentication arrangement agreed with the provider.

props.name: attestation-owner
props.value: Product owner for each customer-facing service, consolidated by the CISO function

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: The service is operated by a provider we do not control and authenticates a population of people who hold no account in our directory. There is no system of ours that could be queried to produce this evidence.

activities.title: Multi-factor authentication, where available, on third-party services holding non-sensitive data
activities.description: Same structural barrier as ism-1679, with an extra judgement no tool can make: "where available" requires establishing that a provider offers no multi-factor option at all. That is a statement about a product's feature set at a point in time, evidenced by the provider, not by our estate.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: The third-party service register, recording for each non-sensitive-data service whether multi-factor authentication is offered by the provider and, where offered, that it is enabled.

props.name: attestation-owner
props.value: Service owner for each third-party arrangement, consolidated by the CISO function

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: The authentication configuration belongs to a provider we do not operate, and the "where available" qualifier additionally requires evidence about what a third-party product offers. Neither is present anywhere in our own systems, so no collector could be written that would answer this honestly.

activities.title: Multi-factor authentication on third-party services holding sensitive data
activities.description: The control is fully addressed by the attestation, but only a human can make it. The subject is another organisation's identity system, and nothing in our estate holds its configuration. Reading our own tenant tells us how OUR staff authenticate to US, which is a different control (ism-1504) and must never be substituted for this one.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: The register of third-party online services that process, store or communicate the organisation's sensitive data, recording the authentication arrangement agreed with each provider and the contractual clause requiring it.

props.name: attestation-owner
props.value: Service owner for each third-party arrangement, consolidated by the CISO function

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: Multi-factor authentication here is enforced by a provider we do not operate, in a tenant we cannot query. There is no API, agent or log we could be entitled to that would reveal another organisation's authentication policy, so this is not a gap that engineering effort closes.

activities.title: The operating system is still supported by its vendor
activities.description: Compares the observed OS release against a vendored end-of-life dataset. Two limits matter. The dataset (endoflife.date) is COMMUNITY-MAINTAINED, not vendor-authoritative, so a date may lag or differ from the vendor's own lifecycle page. And the control says "are replaced" -- this observes whether a system IS supported, not whether an unsupported one is being replaced, which is a project state held outside the host.

activities.title: Application control covers every file type the control lists
activities.description: The control names seven file types. AppLocker has five rule collections, and Microsoft documents what each covers: Executable (.exe, .com), Windows Installer (.msi, .mst, .msp), Scripts (.ps1, .bat, .cmd, .vbs, .js), DLLs (.dll, .ocx) and Packaged apps (.appx). Compiled HTML (.chm), HTML applications (.hta) and control panel applets (.cpl) appear in NO AppLocker rule collection, so an AppLocker-only estate cannot satisfy this control however well configured -- and an organisation that treats AppLocker as equivalent to ML1 application control has a gap it does not know about. Surfacing that is the point of this check. Where App Control for Business is enforcing instead, its code integrity rules are not readable from the collected state and the result is unassessed rather than a guess in either direction.

activities.title: Application control is enforcing on this workstation
activities.description: Observes that an application control mechanism is in ENFORCING mode -- AppLocker with at least one rule collection set to Enabled, or App Control for Business running a code integrity policy. Two gaps are stated rather than hidden. "Implemented" is a judgement about an operational control, and a policy can enforce while permitting everything, so what is observed is enforcement mode rather than efficacy. And AuditOnly is deliberately not counted as implemented: an audit-mode collection writes an event and blocks nothing, which is the most likely way a workstation looks protected and is not.

activities.title: Application control reaches user profiles and temporary folders
activities.description:
This is the control AppLocker's default rules fail quietly. Those rules allow Everyone to execute anything under %WINDIR% and %PROGRAMFILES%; %WINDIR%\Temp is inside %WINDIR%, is the operating system's temporary folder, and is writable by standard users on a default install. So a host can enforce all five rule collections, report thousands of rules, and still let a standard user drop an executable into a temporary folder and run it. The check answers that by comparing the allow rules against the directories THIS host reports as writable by a non-administrator, rather than against a hardcoded list -- an estate that has hardened C:\Windows\Temp is in a different position from one that has not.
What it does not prove, in three parts. It enumerates a defined set of profile, operating-system, browser and email-client locations; a temporary folder belonging to some other installed application is outside what was probed, which is why confidence is partial and never direct. It reads DACLs rather than performing an access check, so ace ordering, inheritance and group nesting are simplified in the direction that over-reports. And it judges only rule collections that are ENFORCING: a collection left NotConfigured restricts nothing anywhere, which is ism-0843 and ism-1657's finding, and repeating it under every control it touches would bury the specific gap this check exists to surface.
An allow rule scoped to administrative principals is recorded but not counted as a failure here, because the control is about locations rather than about whether privileged accounts are themselves subject to application control. A deployment that reads it more strictly -- and at ML2/ML3 it probably should -- sets fail_on_administrator_allow.

activities.title: Web browsers do not process advertisements from the internet
activities.description:
The obvious evidence for this control is Chromium's AdsSettingForIntrusiveAdsSites, and it is the wrong evidence. ASD's own Blueprint states that "Microsoft Edge's native web advertisement capability is limited and does not provide an effective mitigation against the risk of malicious web advertisement", and BlockAds is Edge's DEFAULT value -- so a check resting on it would report every unmanaged Edge installation in an estate as satisfying a control ASD says it does not meet. Chrome's unset default is the opposite (allow advertisements everywhere), and Chromium documents that the blocking value does nothing when SafeBrowsingEnabled is false. All three are recorded as supporting facts and none is decisive.
The verdict rests instead on a force-installed ad-blocking extension, which ASD names as the effective mechanism. The recognised-extension list is deliberately not exhaustive: ASD names uBlock Origin and Adblock Plus as examples while explicitly declining to recommend either, so an estate using a different product is reported as having an unrecognised forced extension rather than as failing.
What this does not prove, in three parts. ASD also names PROXY LEVEL filtering as part of this control, and that is invisible from a host -- an estate blocking advertisements at the gateway will read here as a failure it has in fact mitigated, and that false red is accepted and stated rather than hidden. Forcelist membership means policy requires the extension, not that it is enabled and running in a profile; a non-domain-joined host can only force-install from the vendor store, and a stale extension id after a store migration looks identical to a current one. And a registry value is an administrator's intent rather than the running browser's behaviour.

activities.title: Web browsers do not process Java from the internet
activities.description:
There is no browser policy value that answers this control. NPAPI, the plug-in interface Java applets required, was removed from Chrome in version 45 and from Firefox in version 53 -- note 53 and not 52, because plug-ins kept working in ESR 52, which is exactly the build a conservative government standard operating environment is most likely to have pinned. Chromium's DefaultPluginsSetting and PluginsBlockedForUrls are documented as obsolete and concerned Flash; reading either would be reading a dead key and reporting a pass for a reason that stopped existing.
So the control is answered from which browsers are installed and at what version -- satisfied by construction, with the evidence of the construction recorded rather than asserted.
With one live exception, which is the reason this check exists at all. Internet Explorer never used NPAPI: its Java plug-in was an ActiveX control. Edge Internet Explorer mode runs the Trident engine and supports ActiveX controls. ism-1654 deliberately records Edge IE mode without judging it, because that control speaks to Internet Explorer 11 as a browser rather than to the MSHTML engine. That leaves Edge plus IE mode plus a registered Java runtime as a current, exploitable configuration that every other check in this repository passes, and it is reported as not-satisfied here.
What this does not prove: whether a Java plug-in is actually registered as an ActiveX control. The plug-in CLSID could not be verified against a current vendor document, so the collector emits whatever it finds under HKLM\SOFTWARE\JavaSoft verbatim rather than matching an unverified constant -- a collector that matches a constant nobody confirmed reports "absent" for something it merely failed to look for correctly. Presence of a Java runtime alongside IE mode is therefore treated as sufficient to fail, which may over-report where the runtime is headless.

activities.title: Web browser security settings cannot be changed by human users
activities.description:
Chromium browsers publish every policy at TWO registry paths: the vendor Policies key, which is mandatory and cannot be changed by the user, and a \Recommended subkey beneath it, which sets a default the user MAY override. Both contain the string \Policies\, so the derivation used by the Office macro collector -- a path glob -- would classify a user-overridable default as locked, which is the precise inverse of what this control asks. The collector classifies into mandatory, recommended or preference instead, and this check trusts that classification rather than the path.
The control is a statement about web browsers, plural, so the semantics are EVERY installed browser and not "at least one". A hardened Edge alongside a developer's per-user Chrome installation carrying no policy does not meet it.
Firefox is different in kind. Its only locking mechanism is the Preferences policy, a single JSON document in one registry value where locking is expressed as a Status field rather than as a key path. That document is emitted as raw text and parsed by the evaluator.
What this does not prove, in four parts. A registry value is an administrator's intent, not the running browser's behaviour; only edge://policy or chrome://policy reporting Status OK would show the latter, and neither is readable from a read-only remote query, which is why this can never be direct confidence. Chromium deprecates policy names on a six-week cadence, so a value present in the registry may name a policy the installed build no longer honours. A local administrator can still change anything. And a Firefox estate managed through policies.json in the installation directory rather than through the registry is invisible here -- the two are combined from Firefox 87 with the registry winning, while before 87 the JSON was ignored entirely if any registry policy was set, so a registry-only reading is structurally incomplete on that estate rather than merely unlucky.

activities.title: Internet Explorer 11 is disabled or removed
activities.description: The control is a binary state and both halves are directly observable: whether the optional feature is present, and whether policy disables the IE11 application. The one residual gap is IE mode inside Microsoft Edge, which is a deliberately supported configuration and is reported in the facts rather than judged, since the control speaks to Internet Explorer 11 as a browser rather than to the MSHTML engine.

activities.title: Office macro antivirus (AMSI) scanning is enabled
activities.description: Verifies MacroRuntimeScanScope is set to scan macros, which is how Office hands macro content to AMSI. It does not verify that an AMSI provider is actually registered and healthy, nor that the antivirus behind it is running with current signatures -- so a pass means Office is configured to offer macros for scanning, not that scanning is effective.

activities.title: Office policy blocks macros in files originating from the internet
activities.description: Verifies the ADMX policy state that implements the block, in machine scope and in every loaded user policy hive. It does NOT observe runtime blocking behaviour, does not detect Mark-of-the-Web being stripped by an upstream mail or file gateway, does not cover Office applications outside in_scope_apps, and cannot assess user profile hives that were not loaded at collection time.

activities.title: Office macro security settings are enforced by policy and not user-writable
activities.description: Verifies that macro security values live under the Policies hive and are GPO-delivered, which makes them read-only to a standard user. It does NOT prove a user cannot change them by other means: a local administrator, an MDM policy conflict, or a user with registry write access to the Policies key would still be able to, and none of that is visible from the value itself.

activities.title: Office macros are disabled for users without a demonstrated business requirement
activities.description: Checks that VBAWarnings is set to 4 (disable all macros without notification) by policy. It CANNOT assess the "demonstrated business requirement" half of the control at all -- whether a user who has macros enabled is authorised is an organisational fact held outside the host. A pass here means macros are disabled, not that the exemption process is sound; a fail may be a legitimately approved exemption.

activities.title: Unsupported applications are removed
activities.description: The control names six application families. The vendored end-of-life dataset covers Office productivity suites, two web browsers and Java; searching endoflife.date's 477-product index confirms it carries no entry for Microsoft Edge, any PDF reader, email clients or security products, and browser extensions are not an installed-application concept at all. Those gaps are named in every result rather than omitted, because "checked and supported" and "not checked at all" must not render the same way. Adobe Flash Player is judged from public record instead of a feed -- the control names it explicitly, Adobe ended support on 2020-12-31 and began blocking content on 2021-01-12, so any installation is unsupported without argument. An application that cannot be mapped to a support timeline is reported as unmapped and is neither passed nor failed; and where NOTHING could be mapped the result is unassessed rather than a vacuous pass. Support is judged as of the fact's collection date, so re-running over archived evidence reproduces the verdict that was true when it was gathered.

reviewed-controls.description: Every control in the E8_ML1 baseline at ISM catalog 2026.09.4 is in scope, including those for which no determination can be made.

control-selections.description: Controls in the E8_ML1 baseline with an implemented automated check in this release.

Controls in the E8_ML1 baseline that NO tool can observe: they concern third-party systems, customer identity estates, or approval records. They are in scope and are determined by EXAMINATION of an attestation, never by automated test. Each names where its evidence is held and who owns it.
Controls in the E8_ML1 baseline with NO automated check in this release. They are in scope and no determination is made for them. Their absence from findings means undetermined, not compliant.

resources.title: System security plan placeholder for SYSTEM-GOVDESK
resources.description: This project assesses; it does not author SSPs. The reference exists because import-ssp is part of the assessment-plan model.
